articles.title: Elsie Blundell MP attends Middleton Remembrance service as parliamentary wreaths laid across constituency
articles.excerpt: Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell attended Middleton's service, with wreaths laid on her behalf in Heywood, Castleton, Norden and at Rochdale Cenotaph.
articles.content_html:
Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell attended Middleton's Remembrance Sunday service on Sunday 8 November, while parliamentary wreaths were laid on her behalf across the constituency.

Parliamentary wreaths were laid in her name at the Remembrance Sunday services in Heywood, Castleton and Norden, and at the service at Rochdale Cenotaph.

In a post shared after the services, Ms Blundell said: "Thank you to those who kindly laid special parliamentary wreaths on my behalf at every other Remembrance Sunday service across my constituency - in Heywood, Castleton and Norden - and at the service at Rochdale Cenotaph."

She added: "I am deeply grateful to everyone who led, organised and attended these services, and to all those who came together to remember the service and sacrifice of those who gave everything for our freedom."

Photographs shared with the post show parliamentary wreaths at several memorials, including the Lest We Forget stone for the fallen of Castleton, and a wreath-laying procession.

articles.title: Castleton Remembrance Sunday service draws big crowd but resident asks for a better speaker next year
articles.excerpt: Crowds gathered on Castleton's village green for the Act of Remembrance, but one resident said the words could not be heard.
articles.content_html:
A large crowd gathered on Castleton's village green for the Remembrance Sunday service this morning, but one resident said nobody could hear what was being said.

Castleton's Act of Remembrance began at 10.50am at Castleton Memorial Gardens on Queensway, on the village green. The service was led by St Martin's Parish Church, according to the order of service handed to those attending.

Photographs from the service show people lining the green as the service took place under the trees.

Writing in the Castleton community group on Facebook after the service, Graham Glover said: "Great turnout but please can we invest in a new speaker for next year? You can't hear a word being said."

Castleton's service was one of eight Remembrance Sunday parades and services held across the Rochdale borough today, in Rochdale, Heywood, Middleton, Littleborough, Milnrow, Castleton, Norden and Wardle.

Armistice Day falls on Wednesday 11 November, with the national two-minute silence at 11am.

articles.title: Cranmer Education Trust staff gather for professional development event
articles.excerpt: Staff from Cranmer Education Trust, which operates schools in Middleton and Oldham, convened for a professional development event aimed at improving children's lives through inclusive education.
articles.content_html:
Staff from Cranmer Education Trust gathered for a professional development event called Belong 26 at The Blue Coat School and The Loom in Oldham, aimed at enhancing children's educational experiences.

The event brought together teaching and support staff from the trust's ten schools, including St John’s CE Primary School and Rhodes Green CE Primary School in Middleton.

The focus of Belong 26 was on fostering high expectations, strong relationships, and shared expertise to ensure every child has the opportunity to flourish.

The trust's schools cater to more than 7,500 children and young people across Oldham and Rochdale, prioritising excellence and inclusion in education.

During the event, staff participated in practical workshops covering topics such as inclusive teaching, attendance, safeguarding, and communication. These workshops aimed to equip educators with the tools necessary to understand and address the challenges faced by students, helping them overcome barriers to learning and achievement.

Cranmer Education Trust believes that maintaining high expectations for every child is essential for their success. The collaborative efforts of the staff at Belong 26 reflect a commitment to improving educational outcomes for all students.

articles.title: Middleton's Veterans' Walk: the poppy mural honouring the town's service men and women on Remembrance Sunday
articles.excerpt: A wreath has been laid at Middleton's Veterans' Walk, the Middleton in Bloom mural of poppies, a Spitfire and the white cliffs of Dover.
articles.content_html:
A poppy wreath has been laid at Middleton's Veterans' Walk, the town centre mural that Middleton in Bloom created as a tribute to the town's service men and women, on Remembrance Sunday.

The mural runs the length of a wall in Middleton town centre. A Spitfire trails a stream of red poppies across a painted sky, above silhouettes of soldiers standing among giant poppies, a soldier with a horse, the white cliffs of Dover and a warship at sea.

Planters along the foot of the wall are wrapped in a poppy-print banner carrying the words of Laurence Binyon's poem For the Fallen: "They shall grow not old, as we that are left grow old."

The wreath sits beneath the Veterans' Walk plaque, in the planter in front of the painted sea.

The plaque records that the installation was officially opened on 8 May 2025, the 80th anniversary of VE Day, by Ted Woolley OStJ, branch chairman of the Middleton branch of the Royal British Legion.

Middleton in Bloom finished the white cliffs of Dover section in time for VE Day last year, the Rochdale Times reported at the time. The wooden panel had to be replaced, so the sea was painted first and the Spitfire and poppies were added afterwards.

Elsewhere in Middleton, a "Lest We Forget" display of two kneeling soldiers either side of a cross has been planted with red cyclamen and poppies.

Middleton's Remembrance Sunday parade assembled at 10.10am on Long Street this morning and marched to Middleton Memorial Gardens on Middleton Old Road for a service at 10.45am.

More about the group's work is published at middletoninbloom.co.uk.

articles.title: How many Rochdale servicemen died in the world wars and since? The records give no single answer
articles.excerpt: Between 2,000 and 3,000 Rochdale men are thought to have died in the First World War. No published record gives a borough total for the Second World War or later conflicts.
articles.content_html:
Between 2,000 and 3,000 Rochdale men are thought to have died in the First World War, but no published record gives one total for the borough's war dead.

Rochdale Daily searched the published records on Remembrance Sunday. Different sources give different First World War figures, and none of the sources found gives a borough-wide total for the Second World War or for later conflicts.

First World War

Rochdale Cenotaph, designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens, was unveiled by the Earl of Derby on 26 November 1922. Public subscription raised £29,443 10s, of which £12,611 paid for the memorial. The rest went to a fund for the families of what were then counted as Rochdale's 2,000 war dead.

A later study puts the figure higher. Real Rochdale magazine, marking the centenary in 2018, reported that "approx 3,000 local men died of the 15,000-16,000 who fought in the war", citing Michael Bull's dissertation "Rochdale and the Great War 1914-1920".

The sources do not say whether the two figures cover the same area.

The north face of the Cenotaph reads: "To the memory of the men of Rochdale who gave their lives in the Great War."

Memorial lists are still being corrected. In 2014, seven names were added to Heywood's First World War memorial: W Parkinson, J McIntyre, B C Butterworth, E Collinge, H Armstrong, J Thornley and H Olden. Their links to the town came to light after relatives researched their family trees.

Second World War

The dates 1939-1945 were added to the Cenotaph after the Second World War, and the sunken garden behind it is the borough's Second World War memorial.

No published total for the borough's Second World War dead was found. Smaller records give part of the picture. The war memorial at Rochdale Cemetery lists 54 names from the Second World War, according to the Manchester and Lancashire Family History Society's transcription.

Rochdale Borough Council's list of war dead commemorated at Rochdale Crematorium names 55 service personnel, who died between 1940 and 1947.

Later conflicts

A bronze plaque on the Cenotaph is dedicated "To all those who died in the service of their country".

Corporal Jack Stanley, 26, of The Queen's Royal Hussars, died in April 2012, more than two months after he was injured by an improvised explosive device on patrol near Lashkar Gah in Helmand, Afghanistan. His mother, Brenda, lives in Littleborough.

She said: "Jack was a kind, generous lad with a ready smile." She added: "The world is duller without him and heaven brighter."

Drummer Lee Rigby, 25, of the 2nd Battalion Royal Regiment of Fusiliers, grew up on the Langley estate in Middleton. He was killed near Woolwich Barracks in south-east London in May 2013.

Finding the names

The Commonwealth War Graves Commission's online database lists service personnel who died in both world wars, and the Imperial War Museums' War Memorials Register records the borough's memorials and many of the names on them.

The council publishes lists of war dead buried in eight of the borough's cemeteries and churchyards, including Heywood, Middleton, Rochdale and Littleborough. Families who believe a relative's name is missing from a memorial can contact the council's armed forces team at ArmedForces@rochdale.gov.uk.

The national two-minute silence for Armistice Day takes place at 11am on Wednesday 11 November.

Sources: Rochdale Borough Council; Real Rochdale magazine; Manchester and Lancashire Family History Society; Imperial War Museums; Rochdale Online; Ministry of Defence; Wikipedia's entry on Rochdale Cenotaph. Photograph: Rochdale Borough Council.

articles.title: Remembrance Sunday: parades and services at eight war memorials across Rochdale borough
articles.excerpt: Times and routes for today's Remembrance Sunday parades in Rochdale, Heywood, Middleton, Littleborough, Milnrow, Castleton, Norden and Wardle.
articles.content_html:
Veterans, serving personnel and civic leaders are marching to eight war memorials across the Rochdale borough today for Remembrance Sunday parades and services.

Parades and services are being held in Rochdale, Heywood, Middleton, Littleborough, Milnrow, Castleton, Norden and Wardle on Sunday 8 November. Representatives of the Royal Navy, the Army and the Royal Air Force are joining veterans and civic dignitaries, according to Rochdale Borough Council.

Everyone is welcome at the services and no booking is needed.

Rochdale: the parade assembles at 10.30am outside the Flying Horse Hotel on Packer Street, where ward councillors, magistrates and other civic guests join at 10.45am. It sets off at 10.50am through the pedestrian area to the Cenotaph in Rochdale Memorial Gardens, for a service at 10.55am followed by a march past. The parade then returns to the Flying Horse Hotel and disperses.

In Rochdale this morning, standard bearers, veterans, Army, Air and Sea Cadets, Beavers and a youth band marched from the Flying Horse Hotel to the Cenotaph, where crowds gathered for the service.

Heywood: the parade assembles at 10.15am on Tower Street and moves to St James' Street at 10.30am. It marches along Bridge Street, Market Street, Market Place and Hind Hill Street to Heywood Memorial Gardens on Church Street, arriving at 10.45am, for a service at 10.55am.

At 11.20am the Heywood parade leaves via Hind Hill Street, Pine Street and Hornby Street to Church Street, where the salute is taken, before returning through Market Place, Market Street, Bridge Street and St James' Street to Tower Street.

Middleton: the parade assembles at 10.10am outside the Wetherspoon pub on Long Street and leaves at 10.20am for Middleton Memorial Gardens on Middleton Old Road. The service begins at 10.45am.

Littleborough: the parade assembles at 10.15am at Hare Hill Park and leaves at 10.30am for Littleborough War Memorial, at the Church Street and Railway Street crossroads. The service is at 10.55am, and the parade returns to Hare Hill Park at about 11.35am.

Milnrow: the parade assembles at 10.25am on Harmony Street, moves to Milnrow Library at 10.35am and leaves at 10.45am for the memorial on Newhey Road. The service is at 10.55am, and the parade returns to Harmony Street at 11.20am.

Castleton: a service is held at 10.50am at Castleton Memorial Gardens on Queensway.

Norden: a service is held at 10.50am at Norden Memorial Gardens, at the junction of Edenfield Road and Woodhouse Lane. Part of Woodhouse Lane is closed for 45 metres from its junction with Shawfield Lane.

Wardle: the borough's only afternoon parade assembles at 2.15pm in Village Square and leaves at 2.30pm for the War Memorial on Wardle Road. The service is at 3pm, and the parade returns to Village Square at 3.30pm.

The council has also closed roads for the parades in Heywood, Middleton, Milnrow and Wardle, and has said no alternative routes are provided for some of them while the parades pass.

Mayor of Rochdale Councillor Faisal Rana said: "We are united in our remembrance. Lest we forget."

St Luke's Church in Deeplish is holding a Remembrance service of Holy Communion at 10.30am, led by Revd Natty Gray.

The Royal British Legion's Poppy Appeal ends today. Poppies are available on the Legion's website, at Number One Riverside in Rochdale and at outlets across the borough.

Remembrance events in the borough began with the Festival of Remembrance at Rochdale Town Hall on 16 October. Walkers from Get Together After Serving also completed a 22-mile walk past eight of the borough's cenotaphs to raise money for veterans.

Armistice Day falls on Wednesday 11 November, with the national two-minute silence at 11am. Questions about the parades can be sent to the council at ArmedForces@rochdale.gov.uk.

articles.title: Rochdale man who managed 'Adam' drug line dealers jailed for 10 and a half years
articles.excerpt: Haider Ali, 34, of Pike Street, was sentenced at Minshull Street Crown Court on Monday 9 November after an investigation that began with a drug deal on Baron Street.
articles.content_html:
A Rochdale man who rose from street dealer to manager in the organised crime group behind the borough's 'Adam' drug line has been jailed for 10 years and six months.

Haider Ali, 34, of Pike Street, Rochdale, was sentenced at Minshull Street Crown Court on Monday 9 November 2026.

He was sentenced for being concerned in the supply of cocaine and of heroin, and two counts each of possession with intent to supply cocaine and heroin, covering September 2024 to March 2025.

The investigation by GMP's Rochdale Challenger Unit began after police received information that a drug deal had taken place from a car parked on Baron Street, in Rochdale town centre, just before midnight on 4 January 2025.

Officers followed the vehicle and carried out a reinforced stop when it pulled into a local petrol station. Ali, a passenger, got out and walked quickly away before he was detained.

He was found with more than £1,000 in cash and two mobile phones, which were seized.

In custody, officers recovered two bundles of wraps containing a brown and a white substance, later confirmed as heroin and cocaine. A pre-paid phone taken from him was confirmed to be the Adam drug line.

Investigators found Ali was not only dealing at street level but managing other street dealers, the dedicated dealer phone, and where those below him should make their next deal.

A warrant was executed at his home on 27 March 2025, when he was arrested again on suspicion of possession with intent to supply class A drugs and being concerned in their supply.

PC Joe Cooke, of GMP's Rochdale Challenger Unit, said: “The ‘Adam’ Organised Crime Group have caused misery for many years to the residents and communities of Rochdale and beyond. Haider Ali’s drug dealing as part of this OCG and his management of lower-level street dealers has contributed significantly to the success of the Adam OCG.”

He added: “Organised criminals such as Haider Ali are dangerous individuals with no remorse for their criminality. They operate to exploit the most vulnerable in our societies in order to increase their financial gain and notoriety.”

According to police, evidence showed Ali had progressed from street dealing in 2014 to a significant role within the Adam group by 2024 and into 2025.

Concerns about drug dealing can be reported to GMP on 101 or online at www.gmp.police.uk, or anonymously to the independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

articles.title: Police warn Rochdale homes to lock away family gold after rise in burglaries
articles.excerpt: Burglaries targeting family gold have risen in Rochdale, Oldham and Bury in recent weeks, mostly at weekends, with entry usually gained at the rear of homes.
articles.content_html:
Police are urging Rochdale households to lock away family gold and jewellery after a rise in burglaries targeting it in Rochdale, Oldham and Bury in recent weeks.

Greater Manchester Police said the burglaries have mostly taken place at weekends, during the late afternoon and at night, and warned that offences are likely to increase as the darker nights draw in.

Burglars have most often got in by snapping or tampering with locks or by smashing their way in, while some properties were entered because they had been left insecure.

Entry is typically gained at the rear of the property. Police believe the offenders' vehicle is usually parked on streets surrounding the targeted home.

Detective Chief Inspector Roger Smethurst, of GMP's Serious Crime Division, said: "I would like to remind the public to stay vigilant as the darker nights draw in and ensure their property is secure.

"Anyone with expensive jewellery in their homes should ensure it is safely locked away, out of sight, purchasing a good quality safe which complies with insurance rating standards."

The warning comes as GMP reports that it has been the country's top force for solving residential burglaries over the last 12 months.

The force said 14.3% of residential burglaries so far this year have been solved, up from 9.5% the previous year.

In August 2026 alone, 15.9% of residential burglary outcomes were solved, compared with 9.8% in August 2025, according to GMP.

Crime prevention advice is available on the Greater Manchester Police website, gmp.police.uk.

Suspicious activity or information can be reported to GMP on 101, or anonymously to the independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

articles.title: School-run parking in Rochdale: what the council can do, and what is coming
articles.excerpt: The council has stepped up patrols outside schools and is consulting on School Streets. New pavement parking powers are on the way from the government.
articles.content_html:
Parents across the borough who face double-parked cars, blocked crossings and mounted pavements at the school gates every morning have more options than they may think.

Rochdale Borough Council launched its Stop Means Stop campaign at St Luke's Primary School in Heywood on 28 September, telling drivers to stop for school crossing patrols.

The council recorded 137 cases over the past five years of drivers failing to stop outside schools, including cases where a crossing patrol had already stepped into the road.

It said parking enforcement patrols outside schools would increase, with no fixed schedule, and asked drivers to keep yellow lines and school keep-clear markings free.

Councillor Dylan Williams, cabinet member for highways and facilities, said: “It's really important that people stop.” He described the risk as “a real danger for schoolchildren across the borough.”

A crossing patrol worker at St Luke's said cars parked on the zigzag lines blocked his view and the view of passing drivers.

One longer-term answer is a School Street. These schemes restrict vehicles on the road outside a school at drop-off and pick-up times, so it becomes a space for people walking, cycling or scooting.

Residents, Blue Badge holders, healthcare workers and the emergency services can be given exemptions, according to the council. A School Street can only go ahead with the school's backing, and schools or communities register interest through Transport for Greater Manchester.

The council has consulted on a School Street trial at Smithy Bridge Primary School in Littleborough, with a consultation that ran from 27 November 2025 to 16 January 2026. No decision has been published.

Pavement parking is the other common complaint. On 8 January, the Department for Transport announced that councils in England would get powers to restrict pavement parking across wider areas, rather than street by street.

Local transport minister Lilian Greenwood said: “Clear pavements are essential for people to move around safely and independently.” The department said guidance on using the powers would be published later in 2026.

Since July 2023 the council has also held powers to fine drivers caught on camera committing moving traffic offences, such as blocking yellow box junctions and making banned turns.

Problem parking outside a school can be reported to the council's Parking Services at ParkingServices@rochdale.gov.uk or on 0300 303 8879, Monday to Friday, 8.30am to 4.45pm. Dangerous driving should be reported to Greater Manchester Police on 101 or online, or 999 in an emergency.

Sources: Rochdale Borough Council; Department for Transport. Photograph: Rochdale Daily library.

articles.title: Free Heywood Library friendship group offers a place to meet people this Thursday
articles.excerpt: A free drop-in friendship group at Heywood Library on Thursday 12 November is open to adults, with no advance booking required.
articles.content_html:
People hoping to make new friends or meet others in their community can attend a free friendship group at Heywood Library on Thursday 12 November 2026.

Rochdale Borough Council's event listing gives the time as 1.30pm to 3.30pm at Heywood Library, LCpl Stephen Shaw MC Way, Heywood, OL10 1LW.

The gathering is aimed at people aged 18 and over who want to meet new people or learn skills. The council also lists it as suitable for families with children aged four and over, provided children are accompanied by a responsible adult.

No advance booking is required. Visitors can simply turn up. The listing describes it as a regular Thursday activity and says participants can also find out about joining the library and other activities available there.

For residents who have recently moved to Heywood, work from home or simply want more local company, it offers a straightforward way to meet others without committing to a paid course or membership.

For questions, contact heywood.library@rochdale.gov.uk. Check the council listing before travelling in case arrangements change.

articles.title: Roadworks on Schofield Street in Heywood to begin on 23 November 2026
articles.excerpt: Schofield Street in Heywood will be closed for roadworks from 23 November to 4 December 2026, affecting local traffic and access routes.
articles.content_html:
Part of Schofield Street in Heywood will be temporarily closed for roadworks from midnight on 23 November 2026 until 11.59pm on 4 December 2026. The closure will extend from the junction with Birch Street for 46 metres in an easterly direction, impacting local traffic flow.

During this period, no waiting will be allowed in the closed section of the road. This closure will affect access to Schofield Street, Mount Street, Manchester Street, and Hardfield Street, which may lead to increased congestion in the surrounding areas.

Rochdale Borough Council has announced these roadworks as part of ongoing maintenance efforts to improve local infrastructure. Residents and drivers are advised to plan their journeys accordingly and seek alternative routes during the closure period.

For more information about the roadworks and to view a map of the affected area, residents can visit the Rochdale Borough Council website.

articles.title: RBH tenants rate landlord in top 25 per cent nationally on all 12 survey measures
articles.excerpt: National figures from the Regulator of Social Housing place Rochdale Boroughwide Housing in the upper quartile of large landlords on all 12 tenant survey measures for 2025/26.
articles.content_html:
Tenants of Rochdale Boroughwide Housing, the borough's largest social landlord, rate it among the top quarter of large landlords in England on every survey measure, new national figures show.

The Regulator of Social Housing published the 2025/26 Tenant Satisfaction Measures on Thursday 5 November, covering 356 submissions from landlords with 1,000 or more homes.

RBH set itself a target of reaching the "upper quartile", the top 25 per cent of landlords nationally, and said all 12 of its tenant survey results are now in that band.

Rochdale Daily checked each of RBH's published scores against the regulator's upper-quartile figures, which are rounded to whole numbers. All 12 clear the line.

Overall satisfaction was 80.5 per cent, against an upper quartile of 80 per cent and a national median of 74.2 per cent.

Satisfaction with repairs was 85.2 per cent (upper quartile 82 per cent), with the time taken to complete a repair 80.4 per cent (79 per cent), and that the home is well maintained 82.9 per cent (80 per cent).

Tenants who said their home is safe stood at 88.2 per cent (85 per cent). Those satisfied that RBH listens and acts on their views were 76.6 per cent (72 per cent), and that it keeps them informed 85.1 per cent (79 per cent).

Agreement that RBH treats tenants fairly and with respect was 85.7 per cent, the narrowest margin, against an upper quartile of 85 per cent.

Among tenants who had complained, 48.6 per cent were satisfied with how it was handled (45 per cent). Satisfaction with communal areas was 77.2 per cent (75 per cent), with RBH's contribution to the neighbourhood 79.2 per cent (74 per cent), and with its handling of anti-social behaviour 74.4 per cent (68 per cent).

In a statement, RBH said: "We are very proud to let you know that, across all 12 tenant satisfaction measures covered by our survey, our customers have placed our performance among the top landlords in the country."

It added: "We have only been able to improve by using the feedback and experience from our customers alongside the hard work and expertise of our team and the support of our stakeholders."

"We're pleased that our customers are telling us we're moving in the right direction, and we're determined to continue to learn and continue to improve," the statement said.

The 12 measures come from a telephone survey carried out for RBH by the independent firm Viewpoint. Every social landlord must ask the same questions, set by the regulator.

The regulator advises comparing landlords that used similar survey methods. Telephone is the most common method nationally, used for 65 per cent of surveys of rental tenants.

RBH's claim covers the 12 survey measures only. The regulator also publishes 10 measures drawn from landlords' own records, where RBH's picture is more mixed.

RBH completed 99.6 per cent of required gas safety checks, below the national median of 99.9 per cent. It answered 93 per cent of stage one complaints within the Housing Ombudsman's timescales, just under the median of 93.8 per cent.

It recorded 29.7 stage one complaints per 1,000 homes, about half the national median of 56.8, and reported that 0.2 per cent of its homes fail the Decent Homes Standard, against a median of 0.6 per cent.

Every RBH score improved on the previous year. Overall satisfaction rose from 76.6 per cent in 2024/25.

The results come nearly six years after the death of two-year-old Awaab Ishak, who died in December 2020 after prolonged exposure to mould in an RBH flat.

The regulator downgraded RBH's governance to a non-compliant G3 rating in December 2022. It restored the landlord to a compliant G2 rating in March 2025, after two years of intensive engagement.

RBH's full 2025/26 results and survey method are published on its website, and the regulator's national figures for every large landlord are available on GOV.UK.

Source: Rochdale Boroughwide Housing statement and performance figures; Regulator of Social Housing, Tenant Satisfaction Measures 2025/26. Photograph: Rochdale Boroughwide Housing.

articles.title: The best beauty salons in Rochdale ranked
articles.excerpt: An aesthetics clinic in Norden tops Rochdale Daily's ranking of 18 beauty salons across the borough, scored from 5,374 Google and Fresha reviews.
articles.content_html:
An aesthetics clinic in Norden tops Rochdale Daily's ranking of 18 beauty salons across the borough, scored from 5,374 public reviews on Google and Fresha.

The Aesthetic Rooms on Edenfield Road scored 92.6 out of 100, narrowly ahead of Elements Health & Beauty in Newhey on 91.4. Bare Beauty and Tanning Boutique in Milnrow was third.

Every salon in the top nine is reviewed on both Google and the booking platform Fresha. The town-centre salons with the most Google reviews, led by Pearls on The Walk, take bookings by phone rather than through Fresha, which is why they sit lower down the table.

The top ten

1. The Aesthetic Rooms, Edenfield Road, Norden: 92.6. Google 5.0 from 112 reviews; Fresha 5.0 from 372. An aesthetics clinic offering skin treatments, peels and injectables.

2. Elements Health & Beauty, Shaw Road, Newhey: 91.4. Google 5.0 from 108 reviews; Fresha 5.0 from 256. A day spa offering massage, facials and head spa treatments.

3. Bare Beauty and Tanning Boutique, Dale Street, Milnrow: 87.7. Google 4.8 from 43 reviews; Fresha 5.0 from 958, the most Fresha reviews of any salon in the table.

4. Be Beau With Grace, Norden: 86.4. Google 4.8 from 44 reviews; Fresha 5.0 from 612. Lashes, brows, semi-permanent make-up and training courses.

5. Ella Louise Beautyy, Castleton: 80.1. Google 5.0 from 11 reviews; Fresha 5.0 from 130. A home-based nail and beauty studio.

6. ER Beauty Lounge, Halifax Road, Littleborough: 78.0. Google 5.0 from one review; Fresha 5.0 from 730.

7. Beauty by Jemma, Dale Street, Milnrow: 77.0. Google 5.0 from six reviews; Fresha 5.0 from 98.

8. Lush Beauty N Spa, Oldham Road: 75.8. Google 4.7 from 120 reviews; Fresha 5.0 from 13.

9. Olivia Bells Clinic, Halifax Road: 75.4. Google 5.0 from 12 reviews; Fresha 4.9 from 44.

10. Cwbeautyofficial, Dale Street, Milnrow: 47.6. Fresha 5.0 from 418 reviews; no Google listing found.

The rest of the table

11. NailsByAnabelx, Dale Street, Milnrow: 47.3 (Fresha 5.0 from 384; no Google rating).

12. Pearls Hair, Nails & Beauty, The Walk: 47.0 (Google 4.9 from 365, the most Google reviews of any salon in the table; not reviewed on Fresha).

13. Sleek N Chique Beauty & Fashion Salon, Milkstone Place: 45.6 (Google 5.0 from 120).

14. Elegant Beauty and Nails, Sussex Street: 44.8 (Google 5.0 from 97).

15. Nails By Hediye, Yorkshire Street: 41.1 (Google 5.0 from 39).

16. BZ Beauty Studio, Oldham Road: 40.2 (Google 4.8 from 105).

17. Simply Special, Baillie Street: 40.0 (Google 4.9 from 48).

18. Nia Hair & Beauty VIP, Yorkshire Street: 35.8 (Google 4.6 from 128).

How we ranked them

Every figure was taken from the salons' public Google and Fresha listings on Sunday 8 November 2026. No salon was visited, contacted or paid to take part, and none paid to be included.

Each salon could score up to 50 points from Google and up to 50 from Fresha, making 100 in total. Within each half, 30 points are for the star rating and 20 are for the number of reviews.

The rating points are weighted so that a perfect score from a handful of reviews cannot beat a near-perfect score from hundreds. Each salon is treated as if it had 25 extra reviews at the average rating on that platform across the salons in the table: 4.88 stars on Google and 5.00 on Fresha. The more real reviews a salon has, the less those imaginary 25 matter.

The review-count points rise more slowly the more reviews a salon has, so 1,000 reviews is not worth ten times as much as 100. The most-reviewed salon on each platform receives the full 20 points: Pearls on Google, with 365, and Bare Beauty and Tanning Boutique on Fresha, with 958.

A salon not reviewed on one of the two platforms scores nothing for that half. That is the single biggest factor in the table. Pearls, for example, earns 47.0 of a possible 50 Google points, more than any other salon, but scores nothing from Fresha. ER Beauty Lounge has only one Google review but 730 on Fresha, and finishes six places higher.

Fresha's reviews come only from customers who booked through it, and almost every salon there holds a perfect 5.0. Its half of the score therefore reflects how many customers book a salon online more than any difference in rating.

Facebook was left out. Follower figures could not be gathered reliably for every salon, and the size of a page's audience says little about the treatment customers receive.

The ranking covers beauty, nail, skin and spa businesses within Rochdale borough. Hair salons will be ranked separately. Salons in Whitworth and Shawforth carry Rochdale postcodes but sit in Rossendale, so they were not included. Home-based studios are named by area only.

Ratings change daily, and this table records them as they stood on 8 November 2026. Salons that believe a figure is wrong can send a correction, with a link to the listing, to news@rochdaledaily.co.uk.

articles.title: Woman dies at Tesco in Rochdale after emergency services called
articles.excerpt: A woman in her 50s has died following an incident at a Tesco store on Silk Street in Rochdale on Saturday afternoon.
articles.content_html:
A woman in her 50s has died after emergency services were called to a Tesco store on Silk Street in Rochdale on Saturday afternoon, 7 November 2026.

Greater Manchester Police (GMP) received a call expressing concern for the welfare of a woman inside the supermarket. Eyewitnesses reported that staff initially attended to her before paramedics arrived.

Shoppers were asked to leave the store and the car park to allow emergency services to manage the situation. Video footage showed an air ambulance landing in the car park as part of the response.

Despite the efforts of emergency personnel, the woman could not be saved and was pronounced dead at the scene. A GMP spokesperson confirmed that her family has been notified.

Tesco declined to comment on the incident when approached by the media.

Local readers are encouraged to remain aware of community support services and safety measures.

A spokesperson for EdforAll Ltd stated, "We are committed to working closely with the council to ensure that our hub continues to serve the community effectively." This statement reflects the organisation's intention to maintain its outreach services while adhering to planning requirements.

The need for planning permission underscores the importance of regulatory compliance for community services in Rochdale.

articles.title: How much will Christmas dinner cost in Rochdale? Lidl's £11.11 deal and how rivals compared
articles.excerpt: Lidl is first to price its 2026 Christmas dinner. Here is how it stacks up against last year's Aldi, Tesco and Morrisons deals for a family of four.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale families can buy a basic Christmas dinner for £11.11 at Lidl this year, the first 2026 supermarket price to be announced, with rival deals still to come.

Lidl says its bundle feeds eight for £1.39 a head. For a family of four the shopping list is the same, because the turkey and packs only come in one size, so it works out at about £2.78 each, with leftovers.

The items are on sale in stores from 19 December until Christmas Eve, and Lidl has warned that stock can sell out.

Lidl's basket is a 3kg Birchwood British turkey at £8.85, a 170g pack of sage and onion stuffing at 45p, 15 Yorkshire puddings at 46p and 300g of gravy granules at 99p.

The vegetables are 9p each: 2kg of potatoes, 1kg of carrots, 500g of sprouts and 500g of parsnips. Rochdale Daily has checked that the eight items add up to £11.11.

Aldi, Tesco, Morrisons and M&S had not published their 2026 Christmas dinner prices when this article was written on 8 November. Last year most of them announced in December.

For comparison, here is what each offered in 2025. These are last year's prices, not this year's.

Aldi cut the price of its 2025 dinner for six to £9.31 on 4 December, using the same eight-item list. The turkey was £7.35 and its Super Six vegetables were 5p each. For a family of four that was about £2.33 a head.

Tesco's 2025 dinner for six cost £9.55, but only with a Clubcard. The 3kg turkey was £7.50 with the card, half its usual £5 per kg, and the four vegetables were 15p each. It was sold in most large Tesco stores from 19 December.

Morrisons did not publish a full dinner bundle in 2025. More Card holders could buy carrots, parsnips, sprouts and a swede for 5p each from 18 to 26 December, and 1.5kg of roasting potatoes was £1 for all shoppers.

M&S did not offer a comparable value Christmas dinner, so Rochdale Daily could not price the same basket there.

On last year's prices, Aldi was cheapest without any loyalty card, Tesco came close only for Clubcard holders, and Lidl's opening 2026 price sits £1.80 above Aldi's final 2025 figure.

Loyalty schemes made a real difference in 2025. Tesco's turkey price halved with a Clubcard, and Morrisons' 5p vegetables needed a More Card. Both cards are free to sign up for.

Reduced "yellow sticker" food can also cut the bill. Which? found that Tesco and Morrisons have no set reduction times.

Aldi told Which? that reductions vary by store but are likely near closing time, with fresh food cut by 30% or 75% on its last day. Lidl staff usually reduce items first thing in the morning and a few hours before closing, while M&S reductions are also likely near closing.

Fresh Christmas vegetables and turkeys that reach their date on Christmas Eve are often reduced, but stock is not guaranteed and shoppers relying on it risk going without.

articles.title: Bikers in red leave Birch Services for 13th Ring of Red ride around the M60
articles.excerpt: Riders were due to set off from the M62 services at 1pm to form a giant poppy around Manchester, raising money for Heywood Veterans Association.
articles.content_html:
Bikers in red were due to leave Birch Services on the M62 at 1pm today for the 13th Ring of Red ride, raising money for Heywood Veterans Association.

Riders gather at the westbound HGV parking area of the services, which sit between Heywood and Middleton, before heading along the M62 and joining the M60 at junction 18.

They then travel clockwise around the whole of Manchester's ring road. With every rider wearing something red, the procession is meant to look like a giant poppy encircling the city when seen from above.

Riders could gather from 8am, and organisers said the westbound lorry park would be closed to HGVs from Saturday night until 2.30pm today. More than 1,000 motorcyclists were expected.

Jeanette "Netty" Kiely, who organises Ring of Red M60, told the source the ride was a way of saying "we remember, we care, and we will never forget".

Ms Kiely said seeing the bikes come together each year reminded organisers why they do it. She also praised the Bridge Supporters who stand on motorway bridges in all weathers to wave and cheer as the riders pass underneath.

She added that after 13 years the event had become a community coming together to remember, rather than simply a motorcycle ride.

The Ride of Respect is free to join and non-competitive. It honours members of the Armed Forces past and present and those who died in service.

Money is raised through sales of official red T-shirts, hoodies and patches, with a separate clothing range for Bridge Supporters. Heywood Veterans Association, this year's nominated charity, supports veterans in Heywood, Middleton and surrounding areas.

The Manchester ride grew out of the original Ring of Red on the M25. Ms Kiely has previously said she agreed to stage a northern version after a phone call from the London organiser.

The M60 event's biggest turnout came in 2022, when 5,986 bikes took part, up from 4,400 the year before. Ms Kiely said at the time: "It was incredible to have our highest turn out yet – with 5986 bikes."

Around 3,000 bikers took part last year, according to the Oldham Times. Previous nominated charities include Veterans into Logistics and Veterans in Communities.

Riders finish back at Birch Services once the lap of the M60 is complete.

Source: Ring of Red M60 organisers via the source. Photograph: supplied.

articles.excerpt: Thousands gather across the borough to pay their respects during Remembrance Day services, acknowledging the sacrifices made by servicemen and women.
articles.content_html:
Thousands of residents gathered across Rochdale on 8 November 2026 to participate in Remembrance Day services, honouring the sacrifices made by servicemen and women.

The services took place at various memorials throughout the borough, with poignant moments observed as the community came together to remember the fallen.

Elsie Blundell, MP for Heywood and Middleton North, highlighted the importance of these observances, stating that it is crucial to remember those who served.

Rochdale Council acknowledged the significance of the Remembrance Day moment, reinforcing the community's commitment to honouring its heroes. The phrase 'Lest we forget' resonated throughout the ceremonies, reminding attendees of the sacrifices made for their freedom.

These remembrance activities are part of a national observance, reflecting the collective gratitude and respect for those who have served. The turnout at the services demonstrates the community's dedication to remembering its history and the individuals who have shaped it.

articles.title: Plans approved for 21 new apartments in former office block in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: St James Place on Yorkshire Street will be transformed into residential apartments after sitting empty for eight years, with planning permission granted for the redevelopment.
articles.content_html:
A former office block in Rochdale will be converted into 21 new apartments after sitting empty for nearly a decade.

St James Place, located on Yorkshire Street, has received planning permission from Rochdale Council for the redevelopment, which aims to provide much-needed housing in the area.

Developer Alam Investments plans to create a mix of one and two-bedroom flats, each featuring its own living, dining, and kitchen space. The project is described as a 'sensitive and appropriate reuse of the building', with only internal changes planned to the structure.

A heritage statement was required for the application due to the proximity of the Grade II-listed St Mary’s Ukrainian Catholic Church.

The planning documents noted that the building has been vacant for approximately eight years and is in need of investment and reuse, stating that the proposed scheme will contribute positively to the vitality and regeneration of Rochdale town centre.

This redevelopment is seen as a significant step towards addressing the housing shortage in the area, providing residents with modern living spaces in a sustainable location.

articles.title: Comment: Should fireworks be allowed on any night but bonfire night?
articles.excerpt: Rochdale's council displays went quiet this year, but residents say fireworks carried on into this week. We look at the law, the harm to people and animals, and what could change.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council chose reduced-noise fireworks for its three bonfire events this year, yet residents say the bangs have carried on well into this week. Is it time to ask whether fireworks should be allowed on any night other than bonfire night?

The council's displays ran on Monday 2 November in Middleton, Tuesday 3 November in Heywood and Wednesday 4 November at Cronkeyshaw Common. None fell on Thursday 5 November itself.

By most accounts the Cronkeyshaw display worked: an eyewitness told Rochdale Daily that the quieter, music-led fireworks were enjoyed by a large crowd with little traffic disruption.

The problem is what happens outside the organised events. Residents have reported fireworks through the weekend and into Monday, after the council displays and bonfire night had both passed.

This is not new. In July and August, households in Shawclough and Healey reported explosions after 11pm on consecutive nights, with parents describing children woken after bedtime and pet owners describing distressed animals.

At full council on 15 October, Councillor Jordan Tarrant-Short raised residents' concerns about fireworks being used throughout the year. Councillor Tricia Ayrton said she had been speaking with partner agencies about a coordinated response, and encouraged councillors to raise the call for stronger national action with their MPs.

What the law actually says

In England, adult fireworks may not be set off between 11pm and 7am under the Fireworks Regulations 2004. The exceptions are bonfire night, when the cut-off is midnight, and New Year's Eve, Diwali and the first day of Chinese New Year, when it is 1am. Council-run and national celebration displays are also exempt.

Outside those nights, nothing stops a private display at 10.59pm on any evening of the year.

Shops without an all-year licence may sell to the public only from 15 October to 10 November, from 26 to 31 December, and in the days before Diwali and Chinese New Year. Retailers with a council licence can sell all year round. Consumer fireworks are capped at 120 decibels, and it is an offence to sell adult fireworks to under-18s.

The curfew is enforced by the police, and breaches can bring a fine of up to £5,000. In practice, proving who lit a firework in a back garden at 11.30pm is difficult, and a short burst of noise rarely meets the threshold for a council statutory nuisance investigation.

Scotland has gone further. The Fireworks and Pyrotechnic Articles (Scotland) Act 2022 restricts public use to 6pm to 11pm, with later cut-offs on the main celebration nights, and lets councils designate firework control zones where fireworks are banned at all times.

The physical harm

NHS England figures reported last month showed 161 firework-related hospital admissions in England in 2025, up from 120 the year before. November alone accounted for 85 admissions, compared with 60 in November 2024.

In 2019 a coalition of the British Association of Plastic, Reconstructive and Aesthetic Surgeons, the British Society for Surgery of the Hand and the British Burn Association reported 1,936 A&E visits for firework injuries in a single year. Hand surgeons said they often treat people who have lost large portions of a hand, and children made up 31% of admissions.

The coalition pointed to Northern Ireland, where licensing for the more powerful categories of firework was followed by reported injuries falling from 136 in 2001 to 38 in 2002.

Pets, livestock and wildlife

In the RSPCA's 2024 impact survey, 66% of respondents said backyard displays were a major concern. The charity wants consumer fireworks cut from 120 to 90 decibels, sales limited to licensed shops, and firework-free zones near animals and vulnerable people.

The horse charity Redwings gathered more than 45,000 signatures in seven weeks last year for the same 90-decibel limit.

The National Farmers' Union says sudden explosions are one of the main causes of stress and injury in livestock, and has reported a member losing around four acres of wheat to a stray firework. The borough's Pennine farmland sits close to housing in Littleborough, Milnrow and Norden.

Researchers at Anglia Ruskin University reported last year that crows, rooks and jackdaws abandoned their roosts and flew erratically on New Year's Eve, which the authors linked to prolonged stress.

People with PTSD and anxiety

Help for Heroes and Combat Stress surveyed veterans in 2023. Almost a quarter (23%) said fireworks had triggered a negative experience, from feeling jumpy to panic attacks. Some 74% wanted the days and times fireworks can be used restricted further, and 67% wanted fewer days on which they can be sold.

Unannounced displays on ordinary nights give anyone with an anxiety condition no chance to prepare.

Weddings and New Year

Weddings sit in an awkward place. There is no special rule for them: a wedding display follows the same 11pm curfew as any other private use, on any night of the year, using fireworks from an all-year licensed seller.

For the couple it is one night. For neighbours, a busy wedding season can mean several unplanned displays a month, with no warning.

New Year's Eve is already protected in law until 1am, and few would argue against a midnight countdown. The question is whether the nights either side of it, and of bonfire night, should be treated the same way.

The case against tighter rules

There are serious arguments on the other side. Most people who use fireworks do so legally and safely, and displays are a valued part of family celebrations, religious festivals such as Diwali, and community fundraising.

The NFU itself opposes a complete ban on consumer fireworks, preferring quieter products and advance notice for farms. Opponents of tighter rules also argue that restricting legal sales could push buyers towards unsafe, unregulated products. And the curfew is already widely broken, so a stricter law with the same weak enforcement may change little.

What could be done

The Government's consultation, which closed on 7 October 2026, asked whether the consumer noise limit should fall from 120 decibels to 110, 100 or 90, and proposed reserving the loudest fireworks for professional displays. It did not propose limiting the nights on which fireworks can be used, and its response has not yet been published.

Options that would go further include:

Restricting private use to bonfire night, New Year's Eve and recognised religious festivals, with all-year use limited to licensed and notified displays.

Ending or tightening all-year retail licences, so that fireworks are not on sale in July and August.

Requiring advance notice to neighbours and nearby farms for wedding and private displays outside the permitted nights.

Giving English councils the same power as Scottish councils to create firework-free zones around farms, nature reserves such as Healey Dell, and care homes.

Making quieter fireworks, like those used at Cronkeyshaw, the standard for consumer sale.

Rochdale has already shown that a council display can be quieter and still draw a crowd. Whether the rules for everyone else should follow is a decision for Parliament, including the MPs who represent the borough.

Fireworks used after 11pm on non-permitted nights can be reported to Greater Manchester Police on 101 or online.

Sources: Fireworks Regulations 2004; Rochdale Borough Council; Department for Business and Trade consultation (July 2026); NHS England via ITV News; BAPRAS, BSSH and British Burn Association; RSPCA; Redwings; National Farmers' Union; Anglia Ruskin University; Help for Heroes and Combat Stress; Scottish Government. articles.title: Volunteers wanted for Rochdale town centre's Saturday night Safe Haven
articles.excerpt: Community Medics is recruiting welfare volunteers aged 16 and over for its town centre welfare point, which runs on Saturday nights from 10pm to 3am. Training is provided.
articles.content_html:
A welfare point that helps people who feel unwell, distressed or unsafe on a night out in Rochdale town centre is looking for volunteers.

The Safe Haven, run by Community Medics, operates every Saturday from 10pm to 3am.

Volunteers provide a visible, approachable presence and reassure people who need help. They spot when someone needs support and work with the scheme's clinical team to make sure that person gets the right help.

The role is non-clinical: volunteers do not give medical treatment. Community Medics describes it as focused on early support, engagement and escalation.

No previous experience is needed, and full training is provided in safeguarding, vulnerability awareness and conflict management. Volunteers must be 16 or over and can help regularly or occasionally.

People can apply through the Community Medics website at communitymedics.co.uk/welfarevolunteer, by emailing admin@communitymedics.co.uk, or by calling 0161 806 1533.
